transcript:
Meeting Title: Observability pipeline & token-level metrics deep dive (Halo Labs)
Date/Time: 2025-05-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Tom Becker (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Halo Labs - Lead ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Halo - Infra), Sara Gomez (Halo - SRE)

---

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for carving time. quick agenda: otel/otlp integration, token-level traces, kv cache signals, and dashboards. we'll leave time for q's.
[00:00:12] Priya: thanks maya, excited — we're trying to get better visibility into per-token latency especially when we warm the kv cache vs cold reads.
[00:00:25] Tom: great, we'll show how redwood emits spans and metrics, and how to wire them into an otlp collector and grafana. note: some names might show up slightly different in your exporter, e.g., token-lat vs per-token-lat.
[00:00:40] Sara: quick infra note — halo runs in a locked VPC with egress rules, so we care about private endpoints or otlp over gRPC via a proxy.

[00:01:05] Tom: yeah, that's common. two main patterns: 1) push metrics/traces to your internal otlp collector in the VPC, 2) use a sidecar/agent that speaks http/otlp. we recommend the collector in VPC for security.
[00:01:27] Liam: how heavy is the trace payload? we're worried about token-level spans generating tons of telemetry.
[00:01:35] Maya: good call. redwood emits a small span per request and then subspans for significant phases — token-level timing is aggregated into per-token_histograms and sampled spans for detailed traces. you don't want a full span per token at 100% sampling.
[00:01:55] Priya: can you explain the attributes you put on spans? we want to map them to our billing/latency dashboards.
[00:02:03] Tom: sure — top-level span attributes: model_name, model_variant, deployment_id, request_id, customer_tier, sequence_length, prompt_tokens, response_tokens, quantization_level. For token metrics we emit token_position, token_latency_ms (histogram bucketed), kv_cache_hit boolean, and batch_size. we also add route tags for routing policy.
[00:02:34] Sara: you said kv_cache_hit — is that for prefix cache only or both kv/cache? we sometimes call it "prefix cache" and sometimes "kv cache" interchangeably.
[00:02:44] Tom: in our telemetry we have kv_cache_* which covers both the prefix (request-side) and the long-term k/v cache used for multi-turn. we tag kv_cache_scope: prefix | kv_store. hits increment kv_cache_hits, misses kv_cache_misses and we emit latency for cache lookup.
[00:03:05] Priya: nice. can those be dimensions so we can break out latency when kv hits vs misses?
[00:03:11] Maya: yes — in prom->grafana we recommend panels that compare p50/p95 token latency grouped by kv_cache_hit=true/false and also by quantization_level.

[00:03:35] [00:03:35] Liam: side question on batching: we batch across requests to improve throughput but that can increase scheduling latency for the first token. how is that visible?
[00:03:45] Tom: we emit batch_size and enqueue_wait_ms per request; there's also a batch_fill_ratio and scheduling_delay_ms. those show up as metrics and as tags on traces for slow requests.
[00:04:04] Priya: can we see an example query for grafana to show kv-hit vs miss?
[00:04:11] Tom: sure — example: sum(rate(token_latency_ms_bucket{kv_cache_hit="true", model_name="gpt-embed-x"}[5m])) by (le) for histograms, then compute quantiles. i'll put example queries in the dashboard bundle.

[00:04:38] [00:04:38] Maya: another important bit is sampling strategy: we do adaptive sampling where we keep high sampling for errors or unusual latencies, and low baseline sampling for normal traffic. that keeps trace volume manageable.
[00:04:55] Priya: how do you define unusual latencies?
[00:04:59] Tom: thresholds configurable by customer — default is p99 > 1s for short prompts, or if a KV miss combined with batch_size==1 that triggers higher sampling.

[00:05:20] Sara: what about quantization signals? we run q4 and an int8 baseline across some hosts; can traces reflect performance delta?
[00:05:30] Tom: yes, quantization_level is a span attribute (e.g., q4_0, q8_0, int8). we also emit kernel_exec_ms and allocator_wait_ms per step so you can see where quantization helps. often kernel_exec is lower but allocator_wait can dominate if memory layout changed.
[00:05:55] Priya: great — and does redwood surface per-layer compute metrics or just high-level exec times?
[00:06:01] Tom: currently high-level exec times; layer-level would be noisy and not always portable across backends. we can output more detailed debug traces for bench runs.

[00:06:25] [00:06:25] Liam: on VPC/private considerations: do you have an on-prem agent or do we need to open ports to redwood?
[00:06:33] Maya: for Redwood Private we offer a private control plane and an OTLP endpoint you can peer to via VPC peering, or you can route to your own collector and push only aggregated metrics out. no mandatory inbound ports to your infra.
[00:06:51] Liam: good. so we can keep full traces internal and only export aggregated histograms out?
[00:06:56] Tom: exactly. many customers only export aggregated counters and histograms, keep raw spans internal for security.

[00:07:18] Priya: do you have an example collector config for otlp that filters token-span detail?
[00:07:23] Tom: yes — we'll share an otel collector pipeline example that uses the attributesprocessor to drop token spans or to redact token text while keeping timing. it's part of the artifacts we'll upload.
[00:07:40] Priya: perfect.

[00:08:05] [00:08:05] Sara: one thing we've seen with other providers (Datadog for example) is ingestion cost for high-cardinality tags like request_id or prompt_id. how do you recommend managing cardinality?
[00:08:18] Maya: avoid indexing or high-cardinality tags in metrics; keep request_id only on traces. use derived labels like prompt_bucket or intent_label to aggregate across similar prompts. we also provide token_length_bucket to reduce cardinality.
[00:08:36] Priya: ok, makes sense.

[00:08:55] [00:08:55] Tom: a demo snippet — (screen-share note, paraphrased) here is a synthetic trace: root span 'inference.request' -> 'prepare.kv_lookup' -> 'batch.schedule' -> 'model.generate'. the model.generate has child spans for kv-cache-eval and token-generation aggregated. when a cache-hit occurs, kv_lookup is short and model.generate is faster.
[00:09:20] Priya: do you include prompt hashing so we can reconcile cache performance?
[00:09:25] Tom: we surface prompt_digest but it's hashed and non-reversible; it's safe for indexing and dedupe.

[00:09:45] [00:09:45] Liam: we want to create an alert that fires when kv cache miss rate increases above 10% and p95 token latency goes above 800ms. is that straightforward?
[00:09:55] Tom: yes — in prometheus queries you'd do something like: increase(kv_cache_misses_total[5m]) / increase(kv_cache_requests_total[5m]) > 0.1 and histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(token_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_name)) > 0.8. we'll provide templated alert rules.

[00:10:25] [00:10:25] Priya: can traces link to the grafana panel? like click-through from trace to dashboard?
[00:10:31] Maya: most setups support linking with trace id. our spans include trace_id and we can add a permalink to traces in your vendor (e.g., Jaeger) from a grafana dashboard.

[00:10:50] [00:10:50] Priya: are there pre-built dashboards? we use grafana + prometheus + tempo.
[00:10:56] Tom: yes — we have a starter pack for grafana/prometheus/tempo. includes: token-latency breakdowns, kv hit/miss heatmap, batching distribution, cost-per-token panel (tokens * cost_per_token), and quantization performance comparisons.
[00:11:17] Liam: cost-per-token — where do you get cost numbers? from redwood billing metrics?
[00:11:22] Maya: you can export per-token billing as metrics from the Redwood console or from usage logs. for Private customers you can also approximate using model_variant unit cost exposed as a label.

[00:11:40] [00:11:40] Sara: logging side — we want to be careful about PII in prompts. can redwood redact prompt text in traces?
[00:11:48] Tom: yes — we support prompt_text redaction at ingestion. the collector config can use regex or drop the attribute entirely. we recommend hashing prompt_text to prompt_digest and keeping raw text only if your compliance allows it.

[00:12:10] [00:12:10] Priya: ok. next: performance patterns. when we run multi-turn with a warm kv cache, do you see tail latency issues?
[00:12:20] Tom: tail latency often stems from batch starvation and cache eviction. we recommend keeping an LRU size that matches active user concurrency and monitoring kv_cache_evictions_total. also tune autoscaling/pool sizing.
[00:12:36] Priya: how visible are evictions in traces?
[00:12:40] Tom: we emit kv_cache_eviction events as logs and increment evictions counter; traces around evicted items will show cache miss and higher model.generate time. we also include eviction_reason label.

[00:13:02] [00:13:02] Maya: quick note about kernel selection — our runtime picks kernels based on seq length and model; kernel_switch_ms is another metric to watch because switching can add jitter.
[00:13:15] Liam: interesting, so for bursts with longer sequences it might pick a different execution path.

[00:13:30] [00:13:30] Priya: let's talk sampling rate impact on aggregated histograms — since we sample traces, does histogram aggregation still hold?
[00:13:38] Tom: histograms are emitted as metrics at 100% (summed counters / buckets), not derived from traces, so sampling of traces doesn't affect histograms. we transmit bucketed counts to prom/otel metrics pipeline.

[00:13:58] [00:13:58] Priya: good. how do you correlate tokens in histograms to traces?
[00:14:03] Tom: we include exemplar support: a token latency bucket can attach exemplar trace_id/trace_span to show example slow trace. this requires an OTLP pipeline and tempo/jaeger that supports exemplars.

[00:14:25] [00:14:25] Maya: i'll call out one gotcha — tokenization differences across tokenizers can change token counts; we surface tokenizer_version attribute. if you compare token-based dashboards between vendors, use tokenizer_version to align counts.
[00:14:44] Priya: ah yes, we use tiktoken-ish tokenizer for some models and a different one for others — we'll standardize as part of the bench.

[00:15:05] [00:15:05] Liam: benching — can you run a bench with quantized models and warm kv cache so we can see real numbers?
[00:15:11] Maya: yes we'll run a 30-min bench: 1k short prompts, 200 warm cache entries, measure p50/p95/p99 token latency and throughput. we'll publish the raw metrics and a dashboard.

[00:15:30] [00:15:30] Priya: one more thing: is there a recommended retention for histograms vs raw spans? we want long-term trend analysis but limited storage.
[00:15:39] Tom: metrics/histograms you can retain long-term (months). raw traces shorter (30–90 days) depending on storage budget. many customers keep high-sample traces for 7–30 days and aggregated histograms for 6–12 months.

[00:15:58] [00:15:58] Sara: question: can we add custom labels from our app, like customer_tier inside our request header?
[00:16:04] Tom: yes, you can pass user metadata via request attributes and we map allowed attributes into span labels. watch cardinality.

[00:16:20] [00:16:20] Priya: any tips on dashboards to show batch tradeoffs?
[00:16:25] Tom: show three panels: 1) batch_size distribution over time, 2) enqueue_wait_ms vs batch_size scatter, 3) p95 token latency by batch_size. that surfaces the sweet spot where throughput gains outweigh per-request latency.

[00:16:50] [00:16:50] Liam: will redwood's console export those metrics in a prometheus endpoint or do we have to scrape?
[00:16:57] Maya: for hosted we can push metrics to your prometheus remote write or you can scrape a pushgateway. for private we recommend local scraping or remote write. we'll include both patterns in the collector examples.

[00:17:18] [00:17:18] Priya: one operational gotcha we saw: slow GC in python processes that host the agent caused spikes. anything we should watch for?
[00:17:27] Tom: GC and allocator pauses show up as allocator_wait_ms and process_stop_ms; we instrument host-level metrics too (cpu steal, swap, memory pressure). keep an eye on those as correlated signals.

[00:17:48] [00:17:48] Priya: good. can you show a quick snippet of an OTLP attributes processor to redact prompt_text?
[00:17:55] Tom: sure — (paraphrase) attributesprocessor { actions: [ { key: "prompt_text", action: "delete" }, { key: "prompt_text", action: "insert", value: "<REDACTED>" } ] } or use regex to replace. we'll paste exact YAML.

[00:18:20] [00:18:20] Maya: moving towards wrap-up — any blockers from halo side to run the bench?
[00:18:26] Priya: just getting the sample prompt set and token distribution. liam needs to confirm VPC peering windows.

[00:18:40] [00:18:40] Liam: i've penciled two 1-hr windows next week for peering — will confirm.
[00:18:46] Priya: also want to run a test with traffic that simulates 90th percentile user concurrency.

[00:19:00] [00:19:00] Tom: we'll include a load generator script and config for concurrency patterns.

[00:19:12] [00:19:12] Maya: ok we'll send: otel collector config, grafana starter, load generator, and a small repo with queries.

[00:19:22] [00:19:22] Priya: awesome. couple quick clarifying Qs from sara — are logs and traces correlated by trace id in your platform?
[00:19:30] Tom: yes, we support log->trace correlation. we also add request_id as a first-class field.

[00:19:45] [00:19:45] Sara: on compliance: we need SOC2-type attestations for any exporter that touches PII. do you provide docs?
[00:19:53] Maya: yes, we'll share our security pack and the Private deployment compliance docs; also we can sign an NDA if you want sample configs with real data.

[00:20:10] [00:20:10] Priya: last question — exemplars require prometheus+tempo support, anything else?
[00:20:16] Tom: exemplars require OTLP/Prometheus exemplar support and a tracing backend that accepts exemplar references (tempo/jaeger). we'll document the pipeline.

[00:20:33] [00:20:33] Maya: ok, open floor — anything we missed?
[00:20:36] Priya: maybe mention cost controls — if we sample more traces or export more metrics our ingestion costs go up.
[00:20:43] Maya: yes, cost controls via sampling, cardinality limits, and keeping raw spans internal are the levers. we'll show cost vs fidelity tradeoff panels.

[00:21:00] [00:21:00] Liam: quick note — we'll evaluate the bench results before any capacity commit.

[00:21:08] [00:21:08] Tom: makes sense. we'll try to keep the bench representative and include both cold and warm cache runs, quantized and non-quantized.

[00:21:25] [00:21:25] Priya: thanks everyone. looking forward to artifacts.
[00:21:30] [00:21:30] Maya: thanks all. we'll follow up with links.

[00:21:35] --- brief pause, small side conversation about calendar windows and chasing down VPC approvers ---
[00:30:00] [00:30:00] (call resumed, quick sync on action owners)
[00:30:10] Priya: do you have a recommended default sampling config we can start with?
[00:30:15] Tom: default: 0.05 baseline sampling, error rate 100% for errors, adaptive bump to 1.0 for p99>2s, and keep exemplars for p95 buckets. adjustable.

[00:31:00] [00:31:00] Sara: we might want to integrate with our incident tooling (pagerduty). can grafana alert to pagerduty using these metrics?
[00:31:06] Maya: yes, alerts from prometheus/grafana can trigger pagerduty. we'll include example alert rules.

[00:31:30] [00:31:30] Priya: any gotchas with TLS/mTLS between OTLP endpoints?
[00:31:36] Tom: need to ensure collector has client certs and that the endpoint validates CN. for private deployments we typically use mTLS with a customer CA. we'll share templates.

[00:32:00] [00:32:00] Liam: final perf question: is there a recommended token histogram bucket scheme?
[00:32:06] Tom: yes — we suggest exponential buckets tuned to model latency: e.g., [1ms, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]. works across short and long sequences.

[00:32:25] [00:32:25] Priya: thanks. that's very actionable.

[00:32:40] [00:32:40] Maya: ok wrapping. recap — redwood sends collector config + grafana starter + load gen script; halo supplies prompts + token distribution + peering windows. run bench, analyze dashboards, and reconvene for results review.
[00:33:00] Priya: perfect, thanks.

[00:33:10] [00:33:10] End meeting notes: follow-up material will include sample YAMLs and dashboards.
